title: Meta's Biggest Purge Since 2022 Begins Today. For Indian Tech Workers on H-1B Visas, the Clock Is Already Ticking.
excerpt: Eight thousand jobs vanish in phase one. With more cuts expected by August, the diaspora's most vulnerable workers — visa-dependent engineers — face a brutal 60-day scramble.
body:
On Tuesday morning, thousands of Meta employees across North America woke up to the email they had been dreading — a 7 a.m. message to their personal inbox informing them that their access to company systems had been revoked, their badges deactivated, and their employment terminated.

The Facebook and Instagram parent company began cutting roughly 8,000 jobs on May 20, the first phase of what is expected to be its largest workforce reduction since the bruising "year of efficiency" purges of 2022-23, when 21,000 positions were eliminated. Additional rounds are planned for later this year, with some internal estimates suggesting the total could reach 15,000 to 16,000 — nearly 20 per cent of Meta's global headcount of approximately 79,000.

## The Dread Was Earned

The atmosphere inside Meta in the weeks leading up to May 20 was, by multiple accounts, grim. Former employee Adel Wu described it in a viral post on X as "the most anxious and stressed" period she had witnessed in big tech. Colleagues, she said, had been stuffing bags with free snacks, drinks, and chargers from company kitchens — as if stockpiling for an uncertain future. "Very weird time to be in big tech," Wu wrote.

A software engineer still at the company told reporters they had submitted applications to nearly 250 entry-level roles at other firms after concerns about job security intensified. Despite previous offers from Amazon, Robinhood, and Capital One, the engineer said they were now receiving "zero interviews" — a sign that the broader tech hiring market has tightened considerably. The engineer also noted that Meta's internal AI coding assistant, Claude, was now handling "a lot of the actual coding" as the company pushed to become what it calls "AI native."

Over 1,000 employees signed a petition protesting new mouse-tracking software that Meta introduced to train AI systems, citing privacy concerns. Others described the bitter irony of being asked to help train the very systems that would render their roles obsolete.

## Why Zuckerberg Is Cutting

The layoffs are not born of financial distress. Meta remains enormously profitable, with its family of apps generating record advertising revenue. But Chief Executive Mark Zuckerberg has made an aggressive bet on artificial intelligence, committing between $115 billion and $145 billion in AI infrastructure spending in 2026 alone. The calculus is straightforward: replace human labour with AI capability, pocket the savings — estimated at roughly $375,000 per eliminated role annually — and redirect those resources into building what Zuckerberg has described as "personal super intelligence" for Meta's 3.9 billion monthly active users.

"We are streamlining teams so they are not bigger than needed," Zuckerberg said in an internal memo.

The company's severance terms for affected U.S. employees include 16 weeks of base pay plus two additional weeks for every year worked, along with 18 months of paid healthcare coverage — generous by industry standards, but cold comfort for those whose entire lives are tethered to their employment status.

## The Diaspora's Sharpest Edge

For the thousands of Indian-origin engineers, product managers, and data scientists who form a significant portion of Meta's technical workforce, this round of layoffs carries a uniquely acute risk. India is one of Meta's largest talent pools outside the United States, with substantial engineering and operations teams in Hyderabad and across the company's Silicon Valley headquarters.

Those working in the U.S. on H-1B visas face the most precarious situation. Under current immigration rules, a laid-off H-1B holder has just 60 days to find a new employer willing to sponsor their visa — or face departure from the country. In a hiring market where even experienced engineers report receiving no interview callbacks, that window can feel less like a grace period and more like a countdown.

The ripple effects extend beyond immigration anxiety. Indian tech professionals have long viewed positions at companies like Meta, Google, and Amazon as the gold standard of a diaspora career arc — the culmination of years of competitive examinations, graduate school, and visa lotteries. When those jobs evaporate, the psychological impact reverberates through families and communities, from Hyderabad to Cupertino.

## What Comes Next

Meta's restructuring is part of a broader convulsion across the technology industry. Amazon, Walmart, and Salesforce have all announced significant cuts or hiring freezes in recent months, collectively eliminating over 100,000 positions in 2026 so far. The common thread is AI — companies are spending more on compute and less on people, betting that the technology will deliver returns that human workers cannot.

For India's tech diaspora, the message is becoming impossible to ignore: the era of guaranteed stability in big tech may be over. The jobs that remain will increasingly require fluency in AI tools, prompt engineering, and machine-learning frameworks. Those who adapt will thrive. Those who don't may find that the 60-day clock starts ticking whether or not they hold a visa.
